title: Antonelli makes history as youngest F1 champion at 20 years old
extract: Kimi Antonelli clinched the 2026 drivers' title at 20 years and 68 days by finishing third in a dramatic, red-flagged Mexico City Grand Prix. Max Verstappen won ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton; the race also featured a clash between Ferrari teammates and a suspension-failure crash that stopped the race.

title: China's robot makers have mastered the moves. Now comes the race for brains
extract: Chinese robotics firms are shifting from spectacle-ready humanoid hardware to embodied AI that can understand surroundings, learn tasks and adapt without per-task programming. Reuters reports $13 billion raised across 322 deals in the first half of 2026, as companies compete to collect real-world training data and build more capable robot brains.

title: ‘Anyone can be a super-hacker now’: The world faces a cybersecurity reckoning
extract: An alleged 26-year-old amateur used AI chatbots to help attack nine South Korean banks, exposing financial data belonging to tens of thousands of people. Security researchers warn that accessible AI tools are lowering the barrier to sophisticated attacks, even as the same technology can help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities.

title: Sadiq Khan calls for cap on numbers of robotaxis on London streets
extract: London mayor Sadiq Khan wants Transport for London to gain powers to cap and regulate robotaxis before fully driverless services expand. Current Wayve/Uber and Baidu/Freenow trials still require safety drivers or human intervention; Khan cites congestion, air quality, road safety and taxi livelihoods.

title: AI is stealing Indigenous Australian art and churning out ‘Temu slop’, artist says
extract: Pitjantjatjara artist Sally Scales says AI-generated imitations strip First Nations art of its cultural lineage and agency, with works scraped, altered and sold without attribution. Artists and intellectual-property experts propose stronger data transparency, opt-outs, compensation and takedown mechanisms to protect Indigenous cultural knowledge.

title: National Grid to site biggest substation in UK near planned Teesside datacentre
extract: National Grid has agreed to buy land on Teesside for a proposed substation that could become Britain's largest, supplying a planned 500,000-square-metre AI datacentre. The project could support up to 3.2GW, highlighting the electricity-grid challenge behind large-scale UK AI infrastructure.

title: How a small Wisconsin city scuttled a secretive $1.6bn datacenter project
extract: Menomonie residents helped halt a proposed $1.6bn hyperscale AI datacentre after officials pursued the project through nondisclosure agreements and closed-door steps. Guardian reporting based on interviews, public records and emails details how the 320-acre campus was pitched, how residents organised, and why the project remains paused rather than cancelled.

title: Police use facial recognition to scan one million faces in WA trial leading to 122 arrests
extract: Western Australia police say a five-month real-time facial-recognition trial scanned 1.38 million faces and generated 122 arrests, while recording nine false alerts. Civil-liberties advocates challenge the framing of the error rate and warn of privacy and due-process risks; the vans have been withdrawn while the trial is reviewed.

title: ‘Being hated is very bracing’: Helen Garner on surviving three marriages and being called a ‘rotten feminist’
extract: Australian writer Helen Garner discusses her latest book, The Season, her career in fiction and literary true crime, and the backlash to The First Stone. She reflects on relationships, grandparenthood and finding a wider readership five decades into her career.

title: What we’re reading: Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in October
extract: Ian Rankin recommends a biography of Muriel Spark and a Glasgow crime debut, while Louise Kennedy and Guardian readers share recent choices ranging from China Miéville’s weird fiction to Emma Cline and Halldór Laxness. The roundup offers a varied reading list spanning crime, speculative fiction and translated literature.

title: Unseen Harry Houdini writing published on 100th anniversary of his death
extract: A previously unpublished Houdini article, An Interesting Scrapbook, is appearing in Strand magazine on the centenary of his death. The piece documents the magicians and stage performers who shaped early theatrical magic, revealing Houdini as a careful historian as well as an escapologist.

title: Like many authors, I’m bombarded by scam fan mail. I wasn’t prepared for what would happen when I wrote back
extract: Novelist Joe Dunthorne describes receiving convincing AI-written fan emails that offer to promote his books, then tracing one supposed book-club contact to a Philippine address linked to scam networks. The essay explores how generative AI is making literary impersonation more persuasive and exposing authors to organised fraud.

title: Historian Lucy Worsley looks back: ‘The story of my life has been – the bookworm shall go to the ball’
extract: Historian and presenter Lucy Worsley reflects on childhood reading, her route into history and the role of costume and storytelling in her television work. Her latest book, Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History, draws on the historical subjects that have shaped her career.

title: Yaga review – this erotic witchy thriller starring Hudson Williams is a total head-messer
extract: Sky’s folk-horror mystery reworks the Baba Yaga legend as a coastal Canadian detective story, with Hudson Williams playing two roles and Carrie-Anne Moss as an enigmatic professor. The Guardian review calls it quirky and uneven but praises its supernatural atmosphere and feminist twist.

title: Romeo + Juliet at 30: how Baz Luhrmann made teens fall in love with Shakespeare
extract: Thirty years after Baz Luhrmann’s film arrived, the Guardian revisits its maximalist 1996 adaptation, which recast Verona’s feud as a 1990s gang war and turned Shakespeare into a pop-culture gateway for teenagers. The feature looks at its visual style, soundtrack and lasting influence.

title: ‘Let’s take Alexa out into the garden and smash it with a shoe’: Charlie Brooker and Diane Morgan take aim at Hollywood, AI ... and each other
extract: As Philomena Cunk returns in Cunk on Cinema, Charlie Brooker and Diane Morgan discuss the character’s evolution, the new three-part film series and their comic take on Hollywood and AI. Brooker also discusses his forthcoming deadpan detective series, Blackmere.

title: Saturday Night Live: Obsession breakout Inde Navarrette fronts a scary good Halloween episode
extract: The Halloween episode hosted by Obsession breakout Inde Navarrette features David S Pumpkins, a Midnight Matinees short about a robot companion and a series of darkly comic sketches. The Guardian review calls it the strongest episode of the season so far.

title: Blue Planet III review – David Attenborough makes another absolute corker
extract: David Attenborough narrates the new series, which showcases dolphins using sponges, coordinated shark hunts and a turtle escaping a shark, alongside a stark sequence on coral bleaching. The review praises its mix of wonder, comedy and environmental urgency.

title: The Lives of Others review – Keira Knightley brings star power to Robert Icke’s Stasi drama
extract: Robert Icke’s stage adaptation of the Oscar-winning Stasi drama stars Keira Knightley, Luke Thompson and Alex Dillane. The Guardian finds the production suspenseful but argues that its overt theatricality struggles to match the original film’s quiet psychological subtlety.

title: TV tonight: The Gilded Age returns in all its glossy Julian Fellowes’ glory
extract: Julian Fellowes’ period drama returns with Agnes trying to defend her place in society as ambitious new-money industrialists challenge the old order. The Guardian’s TV guide previews the season opener alongside other Monday-night picks.
